topics.title: Design a Rate Limiter
topics.description: Understanding rate limiting mechanisms, algorithms, distributed implementation, and scaling considerations.

subtopics.title: Rate Limiter
subtopics.theory:
1️⃣ RATE LIMITER

📌 Definition

A Rate Limiter is a mechanism that restricts the number of requests a client can send to a system within a specified time period to protect system resources and maintain stability.

🎯 Why Rate Limiting is Needed

Prevent Denial of Service (DoS) attacks

Protect backend (CPU, DB, memory)

Ensure fair usage among users

Reduce operational cost

Maintain predictable latency

🔑 Important Points

Applied per:

User ID

IP address

API key

Implemented at:

API Gateway (preferred)

Reverse proxy

Application middleware

Works using algorithms

In distributed systems → needs shared state

✅ Advantages

Improves availability

Prevents abuse

Controls traffic spikes

Improves system reliability

Protects database

❌ Disadvantages

Can block legitimate users

Adds extra latency

Complex in distributed systems

Needs careful tuning

🔄 Basic Flow

Client sends request

Extract identifier (user/IP)

Check request count or token

If under limit → forward request

If exceeded → return 429 error

📖 Important Terms

DoS Attack – Overwhelming system with excessive traffic to make it unavailable.

API Gateway – Entry point for all API traffic that can enforce rules.

HTTP 429 – Response code meaning “Too Many Requests.”

subtopics.title: Token Bucket
subtopics.theory:
A) Token Bucket

📌 Definition

In the Token Bucket algorithm, tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate, and each request consumes one token. If no token is available, the request is rejected.

🔑 Important Points

Bucket has max capacity

Tokens refill over time

Allows burst traffic

Controls average rate

🔄 Flow

Bucket starts filling with tokens at rate R

Request arrives

If token available → remove token → allow

If empty → reject

✅ Advantages

Supports burst traffic

Efficient

Simple implementation

Most widely used

❌ Disadvantages

Slight inaccuracies in distributed systems

Requires shared state

📖 Important Terms

Burst Traffic – Sudden spike in requests within short time.

Refill Rate – Speed at which tokens are added.

subtopics.title: Leaky Bucket
subtopics.theory:
B) Leaky Bucket

📌 Definition

Leaky Bucket processes requests at a fixed constant rate, like water leaking from a bucket.

🔑 Important Points

Output rate is constant

No burst allowed

Queue-based model

🔄 Flow

Requests enter queue

Processed at fixed rate

If queue full → drop request

✅ Advantages

Smooth traffic

Predictable

❌ Disadvantages

Drops legitimate bursts

Not flexible

subtopics.title: Fixed Window Counter
subtopics.theory:
C) Fixed Window Counter

📌 Definition

Counts requests in a fixed time window (e.g., 1 minute). Counter resets at window boundary.

🔑 Important Points

Very simple

Has boundary burst problem

❌ Disadvantage

Boundary Burst Problem
User can send full limit at end of window and again at start of next window.

subtopics.title: Sliding Window Log
subtopics.theory:
D) Sliding Window Log

📌 Definition

Stores timestamp of each request and counts only those within current time window.

🔑 Important Points

Very accurate

Memory heavy

❌ Disadvantages

High storage

High CPU

subtopics.title: Sliding Window Counter
subtopics.theory:
E) Sliding Window Counter

📌 Definition

Combines current window count and previous window proportionally to smooth boundary issue.

🔑 Important Points

Balanced solution

More accurate than fixed window

More efficient than log

subtopics.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
subtopics.theory:
3️⃣ DISTRIBUTED RATE LIMITER

📌 Definition

A distributed rate limiter shares request state across multiple servers using a centralized store like Redis to enforce limits consistently.

❗ Why Needed

Multiple servers behind load balancer

Local counters cause incorrect limits

🔄 Flow

Client → Load Balancer → App Server → Redis → Decision

App server reads counter from Redis

Increment atomically

Decide allow or reject

🔑 Important Concepts

Atomic Operation

Operation that completes fully or not at all. Prevents race conditions.

Race Condition

Multiple servers updating same counter incorrectly.

Eventual Consistency

System becomes consistent over time, not instantly.

✅ Advantages

Works with horizontal scaling

Prevents bypassing limits

❌ Disadvantages

Redis bottleneck possible

Hot key problem

Slight inconsistencies

subtopics.title: Hot Key Problem
subtopics.theory:
4️⃣ HOT KEY PROBLEM

📌 Definition

Hot key problem occurs when too many requests hit the same Redis key, overloading one CPU core.

🔑 Why Happens

Popular users

Shared IP addresses

✅ Solutions

Key sharding

Composite keys

Local counters

Edge rate limiting

subtopics.title: Hard vs Soft Limits
subtopics.theory:
5️⃣ HARD vs SOFT LIMITS

Hard Limit

Strictly blocks excess requests.

Used For

Authentication

Payments

Soft Limit

Allows small temporary bursts.

Used For

Feeds

Public APIs

subtopics.title: Final Interview Summary
subtopics.theory:
🎯 FINAL INTERVIEW LINE

A rate limiter protects system stability using algorithms like token bucket, requires shared atomic state in distributed systems, tolerates eventual consistency, and must be monitored and scaled properly.
